newsitem.title: USA: D'Amato to introduce bill to ban US ATM surcharges.
newsitem.headline: D'Amato to introduce bill to ban US ATM surcharges.

text.p: Senator Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, said he would introduce legislation on Wednesday to prohibit banks from charging a second fee on non-customers who use their automated teller machines.
About 54 percent of all automated teller machines now include a surcharge on non-customers, according to a report by the General Accounting Office released by D'Amato at a congressional hearing.
"ATM's were supposed to reduce costs and the savings could be passed on to consumers," the New York Republican said.

"Now, banks are suddenly claiming that ATM's are no longer cost-effective," D'Amato said. "They have decided to soak consumers with multiple fees every time they need to take money out of their accounts."

Until last year, the two largest ATM network operators, Mastercard's Cirrus and Visa's Plus, generally prohibited banks from adding a second charge to non-customers for using teller machines. Banks did receive a fee on such transactions from the customer's own bank.
But in April last year, Cirrus and Plus began allowing ATM surcharges and the fees have rapidly proliferated.

The GAO report found that about one third of banks impose surcharges, covering 54 percent of all teller machines in the country. The survey found that from the end of 1995 to February 1997, there was a 320 percent increase in the number of ATM's with surcharges.
The average surcharge was $1.14 in 1997, up from 99 cents in 1995.
Fifteen states, including Texas, had allowed surcharges prior to the April 1996 policy change by Cirrus and Plus. More recently, Connecticut and Iowa have passed legislation banning surcharges.

Not all the senators at Wednesday's hearing favored legislation banning surcharges, however. Senator Lauch Faircloth, Republican of North Carolina, said surcharging should be left to the market to decide.
"The ATM surcharge is a convenience fee," Faircloth said. "That convenience comes at a price."
